## Why this unit matters

- Differential equations change instant-to-instant, but a computer takes
  **finite steps**.
- We review the derivative as a rate, build the **forward Euler** integrator,
  and analyse its error — local vs global.
- These ideas justify the adaptive solvers used from the ODE chapter onward.

## Equations {.smaller}

A first-order Taylor expansion,

$$
u(t+\delta t)=u(t)+\delta t\,u'(t)+\tfrac12\delta t^2 u''(\xi),
$$ {#eq-s-p03-taylor}

dropping the remainder gives the **forward Euler** update

$$
u_{n+1}=u_n+\delta t\,f(u_n).
$$ {#eq-s-p03-euler}

Local truncation error is $O(\delta t^2)$; over $T/\delta t$ steps the **global**
error is one order lower, $O(\delta t)$ — slope 1 on log–log axes.

## Julia API: the integrator

```{julia}
#| label: s-p03-kernel
#| echo: true
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; β, c, γ, N = p
    λ = β * c * I / N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - γ * I; du[3] = γ * I; return nothing
end

function euler(f, u0, p, δt, tmax)
    ts = 0.0:δt:tmax
    us = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(u0), length(ts)); us[:, 1] .= u0
    du = similar(u0)
    for n in 1:length(ts)-1
        f(du, @view(us[:, n]), p, ts[n])
        us[:, n+1] .= us[:, n] .+ δt .* du     # u_{n+1} = u_n + δt f(u_n)
    end
    collect(ts), us
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]; p = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0); tmax = 40.0
_, us = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, 0.1, tmax); round.(us[:, end]; digits = 2)
```

## Generated result: convergence

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-p03-convergence
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Global error of forward Euler at $t=40$ vs step size. Measured points parallel the slope-1 reference, confirming $O(\\delta t)$ convergence."
using CairoMakie
δt_ref = tmax / 2^16; _, us_ref = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, δt_ref, tmax); u_ref = us_ref[:, end]
δts = [tmax / 2^k for k in 6:11]
errs = map(δts) do δt
    _, u = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, δt, tmax); maximum(abs.(u[:, end] .- u_ref))
end
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10,
          xlabel = "δt", ylabel = "global error at t = 40")
scatter!(ax, δts, errs; markersize = 12, color = :firebrick, label = "measured")
lines!(ax, δts, errs[1] .* (δts ./ δts[1]); linestyle = :dash, color = :black, label = "slope 1")
axislegend(ax; position = :rb); fig
```

## Validation

Empirical order (successive halvings) should be ≈ 1, and Euler preserves the
conservation law at any step:

```{julia}
#| label: s-p03-check
#| echo: true
orders = [log2(errs[k] / errs[k+1]) for k in 1:length(errs)-1]
mean_order = sum(orders) / length(orders)
_, uc = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, 0.5, tmax)
cons_ok = all(t -> isapprox(t, 1000.0; atol = 1e-9), vec(sum(uc; dims = 1)))
(round(mean_order; digits = 3), isapprox(mean_order, 1.0; atol = 0.1), cons_ok)
```

## Limitations & takeaways

- Accuracy improves only **linearly** — halving the error doubles the cost.
- Forward Euler is only **conditionally stable**: too-large steps oscillate or
  diverge on stiff problems.
- Adaptive higher-order methods (`Tsit5`, …) get far more accuracy per unit work.
- **Takeaway:** understand order and stability, then let SciML choose the step.

::: {.notes}
Draw the distinction between local truncation error and accumulated global error
explicitly; the one-order drop is the crux. Note the reference solution is a very
fine Euler run, so we measure convergence to Euler's own limit. Mention that this
motivates adopting Tsit5 and adaptive stepping from the ODE chapter, and invite
learners to try the midpoint method in the notebook to see order 2.
:::
